newsitem.title: IRAQ: Oil companies flock to Baghdad to buy crude.
newsitem.headline: Oil companies flock to Baghdad to buy crude.

text.p: An Iraqi oil official from the State Organisation for the Marketing of Oil (SOMO) said foreign firms were flocking to Baghdad to finalise deals for the purchase of Iraqi crude under the oil-for-food formula with U.N.

"Many companies arrived today and many more are on their way. We wrote to all those who dealt with us in the past and the response has been very positive," the official, refusing to be named, told Reuters.
He said representives from France's Elf Aquitaine and Japan's Mitsubishi were among those companies in Baghdad seeking shipments of Iraqi crude.
"Not only Elf and Mitsubishi which could be the first to load Iraqi crude. There are many other firms in Baghdad," he said.
"Demand for our oil is much higher than what we could be allowed to export under the deal with U.N."
He said the quantity Iraq would be allowed to export depends on prevalent prices whose surge recenly lowered the limited amounts from around 800,000 to about 550,000 barrels per day in six months.
Two experts from the Dutch firm Saybolt arrived in Baghdad on Tuesday to see whether Iraq's oil gauging equipment on the border with Turkey was working properly.
The official newspaper al-Qadissiya said the experts went to Zakho on the Turkish border to "put the final touches" on preparations for the oil exports.

"Iraq succeeded...in making available and in a short period of time all the metering equipment and instruments as well as computers and gauging devices neeeded to make the flow of oil a success," the paper said, quoting SOMO chairman Saddam Hassan.
The experts were expected in Baghdad on Thursday. They will report to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on their findings later in the week.
The visit by the Saybolt experts is part of preparations for the flow of partial Iraqi exports worth $2 billion in six months under the oil deal whose terms Baghdad accepted on November 25.

A team from Lloyd's Shipping Intelligence left Baghdad on Tuesday following an inspection tour of Iraq's trade outlets to pave the way for future U.N. inspection of humanitarian supplies reaching Iraq under the oil deal.
